content.title: Response to Reviewer RduT
content.comment:
We thank Reviewer RduT for positive comments and helpful feedback on our work. We address many of Reviewer RduT’s suggestions in the general response above and respond to specific comments below.

**Justification of novelty & paper organization.**

*“The novelty of this paper is minor. The presented method is just a natural combination with FL and LNL methods. Can the author further describe the unique challenge to apply the LNL method to the FL setting?”*

We thank Reviewer RduT’s suggestion. We update the manuscript in Section 1 to describe the challenge in more depth related with applying the LNL method to the FL setting. The motivation of this paper is to propose a solution to the existing noisy label learning problem applied in federated scenarios. And FedDual is a model structure that makes existing label learning methods more efficient. In this paper, we are not simply extending the centralized label learning approach to federated scenarios. First of all, different from the centralized noise label learning problem, we find that the performance of the trained federated learning model will be broken by the noise label in nonIID distribution. In order to solve this challenge, we have tried to directly apply the existing centralized noise label learning method to federated learning setting (PCORES, PKNN), but the effect is very poor. Therefore, we propose the FedDual method to perform better in federated setting with noise labels (FedCORES, FedKNN, FedTwinKNN, FedKNNpretrain). In our paper, we compare the FedDual method (FedCORES, FedKNN, FedTwinKNN, FedKNNpretrain) with the noise label learning method directly applied to federated learning (PCORES, PKNN) as shown in Table 1 and Table 2, showing the effectiveness of the FedDual method.

**Paper Organization**

*“Some important related work is missed. For example, a prior work[1] presents to use mixup to mitigate the local noise effect in the FL setting. Their relationship and empirical comparisons should be discussed.”*

We thank the reviewer for raising this point and we will consider your suggestions carefully. Could you please list the reference for me? Only with general description for the reference, it’s not enough for me to locate the paper.

We thank Reviewer RduT for the suggestion to improve paper organization. We have modified the manuscript and refer the reviewer to the general response above, where we detail the structural changes that were made.

content.summary_of_the_paper: In this manuscript, the authors attempt to tackle the client-dependent label noise issue that is possible to occur in federated learning. They proposed a general framework FedDual, which boils down to using existing methods to select samples that are likely to have noisy labels that are equal to their clean labels, and using the gradients of those samples to update the global model.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Pros:
1. The authors proposed an intuitive framework for learning with noisy samples under federated settings.

2. The empirical performance of the authors' proposed method is significant compared with selected baseline methods.

3. Authors systematically introduced the generation scheme of label noise under a federated learning setting, which is non-trivial.

Cons:
1. Authors should explicitly discuss what prevents existing label noise learning methods to be applied under federated settings, even though the label noise is client-dependent, why can't we apply updating scheme similar to FedAvg to learn a label-noise learning method that aggregates the client-dependent information? Using BLTM [1] as an example, why can't we train each client-biased transition matrix estimator locally, and using their gradients to learn a global unbiased transition matrix estimator?

2. The theoretical novelties and insights FedDual brought is limited, filtering samples that are likely to be noisy is a very intuitive solution, the difficult part is how to achieve that. The three solutions authors proposed are mostly based on existing works [2, 3].

3. The collection of baseline methods need to be expanded, the highly related existing work such as FedCorr [4] and more label noise learning methods should be added for comparsion, among the five baselines, only two of them (CORES, loss correction) are label noise learning methods.

[1] Yang, S., Yang, E., Han, B., Liu, Y., Xu, M., Niu, G., & Liu, T. (2022, June). Estimating instance-dependent bayes-label transition matrix using a deep neural network. In International Conference on Machine Learning (pp. 25302-25312). PMLR.

[2] Cheng, H., Zhu, Z., Li, X., Gong, Y., Sun, X., & Liu, Y. (2020). Learning with instance-dependent label noise: A sample sieve approach. arXiv preprint arXiv:2010.02347.

[3] Han, B., Yao, Q., Yu, X., Niu, G., Xu, M., Hu, W., ... & Sugiyama, M. (2018). Co-teaching: Robust training of deep neural networks with extremely noisy labels. Advances in neural information processing systems, 31.

[4] Xu, J., Chen, Z., Quek, T. Q., & Chong, K. F. E. (2022). FedCorr: Multi-Stage Federated Learning for Label Noise Correction. In Proceedings of the IEEE/CVF Conference on Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (pp. 10184-10193).
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
Clarity: This manuscript is well-written and clearly structured, and ideas are easy to follow.

Quality: The quality of this manuscript is good.

Novelty: As I mentioned above, the novelty of this paper is somewhat limited, the FedDual is an intuitive solution, but not novel. Besides the idea of "selecting confident samples locally, use them to train the global network", the authors didn't propose anything that carries significant insights, the mentioned three confident sample estimation methods are mostly based on existing works.

Reproducibility: The authors are encouraged to release the implementation code for reviewers to check the reproducibility.
content.summary_of_the_review: Overall, the authors are studying an important and interesting question. And the general framework (selecting confident samples locally, and using them to train a better global network) is sound and intuitive. However, the novelties this manuscript provided is limited. And the experiments are not comprehensive enough to convince me of the superiority of their proposed method. Based on those reasons, and the selectivity of this venue, I vote for the rejection of this paper.

content.comment:

*“Authors should explicitly discuss what prevents existing label noise learning methods to be applied under federated settings, even though the label noise is client-dependent, why can't we apply updating scheme similar to FedAvg to learn a label-noise learning method that aggregates the client-dependent information? Using BLTM [1] as an example, why can't we train each client-biased transition matrix estimator locally, and using their gradients to learn a global unbiased transition matrix estimator?”*

We thank Reviewer 5KcH’s suggestion. We update the manuscript in Section 1 to describe the challenge in more depth related to applying the LNL method to the FL setting.

- The motivation of this paper is to propose a solution to the existing noisy label learning problem applied in federated scenarios. The main reason preventing existing label noise learning methods to be applied under a federated setting is that with insufficient sample size and possibly an incomplete observed label space (in the non-IID setting) at each local client, the centralized learning-based methods tend to overfit the corrupted samples and recognize the noisy samples as clean samples. Therefore, it is challenging to avoid model overfitting and effectively recognize wrongly labeled samples from different clients in FL. And FedDual is a model structure that makes existing label learning methods more efficient. In this paper, we are not simply extending the centralized label learning approach to federated scenarios. First of all, different from the centralized noise label learning problem, we find that the performance of the trained federated learning model will be broken even more by the noise label in nonIID distribution. To solve this challenge, we have tried to directly apply the existing centralized noise label learning method to a federated learning setting (PCORES, PKNN), but the effect is very poor. Therefore, we propose the FedDual method to perform better in federated settings with noise labels (FedCORES, FedKNN, FedTwinKNN, FedKNNpretrain). In our paper, we compare the FedDual method (FedCORES, FedKNN, FedTwinKNN, FedKNNpretrain) with the noise label learning method directly applied to federated learning (PCORES, PKNN) as shown in Table 1 and Table 2, showing the effectiveness of the FedDual method.

- The idea that training each client-biased transition matrix estimator locally, and using their gradients to learn a global unbiased transition matrix estimator is similar to ours. What the two ideas have in common is to get more prior knowledge to better filter out the noise locally. However, our method is to obtain the global noise label information from the model training, but your idea is by obtaining the global noise transfer matrix estimation. This idea looks fantastic, and we will consider integrating your ideas to expand FedDual in the future.

content.title: Comment on authors response
content.comment:
I appreciate authors' detailed rebuttal. However, the authors did not make arguments that are convincing enough regarding the novelty of this manuscript. 

1. Indeed, FedDual is more of a general framework, and I agree that proposing a general framework accounts for some contribution. However, to make this distribution non-trivial, I expect enough novelties or technical insights. The idea of filtering noisy samples lacks novelty and is too naive. This contribution is not enough for an ICLR paper in my opinion.

2. The filtering procedure is not insightful enough. For this contribution to be significant, authors should propose a novel method for local filtering that is intuitively sound.

In addition to the insufficient novelties, authors should also address some of the unclear points made in the rebuttal:

1. Authors mentioned the label space could be incomplete for each client, while I agree with this premise, I fail to see how FedDual can address this issue.

2. Why is FedDual more efficient? Is there asymptotic analysis and empirical evidence to support this claim?

Overall, I think this manuscript still needs improvements, specifically, authors should consider how to insightfully devise a P model to filter noisy samples locally. I believe there are better ways.

Based on the suggestion from Reviewer, we provide a preliminary version that seems promising in Appendix C.3 which includes more discussion on the contribution of the P and G models to the overall performance. The P model is used to help the G model select clean samples, so the metric to measure the performance of the P model should be the F-score value of the noise label sample filtering. The G model is applied to real tasks, so the measure of G model performance should be prediction accuracy. In this paper, we demonstrate the performance of the baseline method FedAvg in the section 5.2, that is, the result of filtering noise label samples for the G model without a P model. In addition, the performance of the P model was also demonstrated experimentally in the section 5.3. As shown in Figure 4, we show the pure ratio distribution of P models on different algorithms.

**Clarification.**

*“Federated learning scenarios are very sensitive to on-device resources. It seems to me that there is a significant added computation cost on the end devices. The paper should clarify this.”*

We thank Reviewer 6Nsr for the suggestion to clarify computation cost on the end device for FedDual. We updated manuscript in Appendix C.4 for this suggestion. In FedDual, it is at an additional computational cost that P model helps G model to select clean samples. Besides, it has different cost for different dual model structure. Because that P model is constructed from the trained model, the additional computational cost of P-model denoising will be so small that it can be ignored in Structure (1) (2). For structure (3), P model is constructed by training locally so that it will show the larger cost than the previous two structures. In general, the extra computational cost is necessary to help the model filter out noisy label samples, which results in better performance of the trained model and faster model convergence. 

**Clarification.**

*“I think it is necessary to see the effect of client participation rate and data heterogeneity level on the performance of the dual model algorithm.”*

Actually, we have displayed the specific experiment results in our paper. We have changed the description to make it clearer in Section 5. 

1. As shown in Table 1 and Table 2, the fraction of selected clients on CIFAR10 per round C = 1, and the fraction of selected clients on CIFAR100 and MNIST per round C = 0.1. 

2. We also display the performance of FedDual in IID and nonIID distribution in the Table 1 and Table 2. Furthermore, we show the performance of the dual model algorithm on different data heterogeneity level on Figure 5. 

**Paper organization**

*“The paper does feel a bit incoherent and some experimental setup information is difficult to find. It is not clear to me how the P-model is trained in different settings; which dataset does it use when using a pre-trained model?”*

We thank reviewer 6Nsr for raising attention with experimental setup. We’ve clarified our wording in the Section 4.2 to make it clear for reader to understand how P model works in different type of dual model structure. In addition, we extend more experimental setup information in Appendix B.2. Specifically，the pre-trained model in the dual model structure I can be acquired from training ResNet18 model on the ImageNet dataset.

content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength

The paper considers federated learning with heterogeneous noisy labels, which may be practically useful. The proposed method is tested on multiple benchmark datasets with heterogeneous label noise in different clients and is shown to outperform baseline methods.

Weaknesses

The first concern is about the convergence of the proposed method. As the proposed method is based on a dual model architecture, where the P model is a local and personalized denoising model and helps the G model select clean samples which are used to train G model later, the rate of label noise and the selection quality of clean samples may inevitably affect training, how can we guarantee the convergence of proposed method?

Another concern is that the two noise models, i.e., add noise and then divide clients, and divide clients then add noise seem artificial. They may happen together in real-world cases. Could the authors provide more real-world examples to just these two models?

Also, label noise learning is a very hot research topic in centralized learning and the idea of selecting clean (less noisy) data is not new. Extending it to the federated setting seems straightforward.

content.title: Response to Reviewer ddDJ
content.comment:
We thank Reviewer ddDJ for the positive comments and helpful feedback on our work. We address many of Reviewer ddDJ’s suggestions in the general response above and respond to specific comments below.

**Convergence discussion.**

*“The first concern is about the convergence of the proposed method…… How can we guarantee the convergence of the proposed method?”*

We thank the reviewer for raising this point. Below, we provide a preliminary version of our updated manuscript that seems promising and includes an additional interpretation of the convergence for our proposed method in Appendix Section C.2. 

1. In Section 5.2, we explore the effect of the label noise rate on the performance of the G model. Consider an extreme case where there is no P model to select noise labels for the G model, that is, G models trained by FedAvg strategy, then G models will gradually diverge with the increasing label noise rate, refer to Figure 1 (b) in the Introduction section of the article. In addition, if the P model helps the G model to effectively denoise, it will reduce the influence of label noise in federated learning, thereby further improving the convergence performance of the G model. Therefore, with increasing label noise rate, the convergence tends of FedDual and FedAvg are consistent to gradually diverge and is convergent than FedAvg. In section 5.2, we also prove it in Table 1 and Table 2. 

2. In Sections 5.2 and 5.3, we explore the effect of the quality of clean samples selected by the P model on the performance of the G model. There are three types of dual model structure and two instantiated label noise learning methods in FedDual. On the one hand, we discuss horizontally the performance differences instantiated into FedDual by different label noise learning methods (i.e., CORES, KNN-based denoising methods), see Table 2. On the other hand, we also compare vertically the performance differences of the specific label noise learning method instantiated into three types of dual model structure in Table 2 and Figure 4.

**Real-world examples of two noise models.**

*“Could the authors provide more real-world examples to just these two models?”*

We thank Reviewer ddDJ’s suggestions for Real-world examples to two noise models. We provide a preliminary version that seems promising in Appendix A.1 which includes more discussion on the real-world examples to just these two models. 

Social media such as Twitter allows users to tag their own posts, and these tags can be seen as the label. Assuming that the social media platform hopes to realize the recognition of user pictures through federated learning and support automatic tagging on local mobile devices, it will face the problem of the non-iid and noisy label. On the one hand, users have their preferences, the types and amounts of pictures posted are different, which brings non-iid issues; on the other hand, users may label the pictures they posted incorrectly, and bring noisy data for the federated learning process.

For the label noise described in the ANDC model, tangerines are usually mislabeled as orange, or Alaska is mislabeled as a husky, these kinds of mislabelling are quite common for all users because the tagged objects themselves are similar, and most users have a similar probability to label wrong, i.e., the label noise distribution among users follow the same distribution; But for label noise in the DCAN model, as is illustrated in Figure 7, the first user marked Monet’s painting as Picasso’s, because he remembered a wrong name, while the second user marked the movie produced by Marvel Studios, LLC as produced by DC Studios, Inc., because she doesn’t care about superheroes in the movie industry. These kinds of mislabelling are personalized because different users have different knowledge structures which lead to different mislabeling modes, thus the label noise distribution is quite different among users.

content.title: Response to all reviewers
content.comment:
We thank the reviewers for their thoughtful and constructive review of our manuscript. We were encouraged to hear the reviewers found the federated learning with noisy labels problem we present to be both interesting (Reviewers ddDJ, 5KcH, RduT) and novel (Reviewer 6Nsr) and that they view our methodology as useful (Reviewer ddDJ), novel (Reviewer 6Nsr), significant (Reviewers 5KcH) and easy to implement (Reviewer RduT). In response to feedback, we provide a general response here to points raised by multiple reviewers, individual responses below to address each reviewer’s concerns, and an updated manuscript.
Regarding questions from Reviewers ddDJ, 5KcH, and RduT about novelty and technical contributions, we emphasize that the two key contributions of this work are (1) designing a novel dual structure approach FedDual for effectively training federated learning model with heterogeneous label noise, where each client maintains a local and personalized denoising model, in addition to the globally shared model, and (2) proposing three ways to construct the P model according to the different way to combine information from the global model or other pre-trained models. 
1. Prior works [1-5] are often studied in centralized learning and cannot be directly applied to FL. To the best of our knowledge, we first propose an FL framework with a dual model structure named FedDual which can effectively deal with noisy label challenges on FL.
2. Prior approaches [6-10] are either select recognized low-noise level clients which still bring in many label noise samples or are often complex with more stages to pre-process or fine-tune global models. We address this by introducing a simple and effective dual model structure that has not been previously used for federated learning with heterogeneous label noise. We demonstrate through experiments with our label noise generation schemes that FedDual often outperforms prior methods.

As summarized by the Reviewer, we formalize federated learning with heterogeneous label noise and hold significant importance for future work. We introduce a dual model algorithm to filter and learn from data with label noise as well which is original work to the best of my knowledge.

In response to comments from Reviewers 6Nsr and 5KcH about the motivation and detail of experiments, we have updated our manuscript to include a larger, more diverse set of explanations. As demonstrated in Sections 5.1 and 5.2, we present substantial experiments to demonstrate that FedDual can effectively recognize heterogeneous label noise in different clients and improve the performance of the aggregated model. We also include more discussion on the contribution of the P and G models to the overall performance in Appendix C.3. Regarding feedback from Reviewers ddDJ, 6Nsr, and 5KcH about the details of FedDual, we provide a preliminary version in our updated manuscript that seems promising. It includes an additional interpretation of the convergence for our proposed method in Appendix Section C.2. We also clarify the computation cost on the end device for FedDual in Appendix C.4.
We have made the following changes.

1. Introduction (Section 1): We have added explanations for motivation about our problem setting and description to highlight our contribution and novelty.
2. Figure 1 (Section 1): Figure 1 provides an overview of the experiments: explore the influence of heterogeneous noise labels on the FL model. We have edited the figure and caption to better communicate our contributions.
3. Conclusion (Section 7): We have updated the conclusion to include directions for future work.
4. Appendix: We have updated the appendix to include more explanation of data generation models (A). We also updated the appendix to include an extended discussion of the convergence of FedDual (C.1), an extended discussion of the contribution of the G model and P model (C.2), an extended discussion of the computation cost of FedDual (C.3). At last, we extend more description about experimental setup (B.2).

In summary, as federated learning become increasingly widespread in use, federated learning with heterogeneous label noise will become one critical research, where the robust federated learning model should be built for real application task even though in heterogeneous noise label distribution. We hope that FedDual will facilitate the development of effective systems for this task and that future work will build on our proposed method.

We would again like to thank all reviewers for their time and feedback, and we hope that our changes adequately address all concerns.

content.title: Paper Decision
content.metareview:_summary,_strengths_and_weakn:
The paper studies Federated learning settings where the data labels have variable noise. It is special case of heterogeneous distribution in federated setting. The idea of using a device specific de-noising model was proposed and experiments on 3 standard small vision task (MSNIT and CIFAR) showed benefits of using the method in this settings. 

Federated learning with variable data distrbution is now a very well studied topic. Managing data distribution with a variety of ideas has been in the machine learning literature for quite some time. As a result, merely showing benefits on small standard dataset in a limited constraints environment does not comprise as enough contribution for an ICLR conference.  The paper needs to bolster its claims by more rigorous and thorough analysis, either empirical or theoretical.
content.summary_of_AC-reviewer_meeting:
As pointed out by reviewers, the authors need to justify the setting with enough real world examples. Currently, there is none. Ideally, the experiments in the paper counts as simulated experiments because the setting itself is simulated on real datasets. The paper needs more analysis on the practicality of the scenarios and some more rigorous stress testing to understand the weak regions of the proposed methods. 
There cannot be a silver bullet solution that works across all the regions.
